themes.title: AI Capex: Growth Now Funded With Debt
themes.status_note: Still Fading: QQQ fell 3.1% in a month as Meta's negative free cash flow and AI credit stress hit the trade.
themes.summary: AI spending is no longer a pure demand story. QQQ returned -3.12% over one month against -0.27% for the S&P 500, and Meta is down 17.5% over the month, including a 6.98% drop after it reported negative free cash flow, $135-145 billion of 2026 capex and a new non-voting share class to raise money. CoreWeave's credit default swaps trade above 1,000 basis points and its 2031 bond yields about 15.6%. Nvidia says demand is off the charts but capital is scarce. Fading means financing, not demand, is now the constraint; a one-week rebound does not reverse that.
themes.body_text:
QQQ closed at $721.25 on October 27. It lost 3.12% over one month while the S&P 500 lost 0.27%, and the semiconductor ETF SMH fell 8.01%. The weakness is concentrated in the companies paying for the build-out: Meta fell 17.49% over the month, Alphabet 6.79%, AMD 11.16%, Micron 14.18% and Vertiv 17.66%.

The trigger was Meta's October 21 third-quarter report. Capital spending for 2026 is now $135-145 billion, free cash flow was negative $2.12 billion, and the company created a Class C non-voting stock explicitly to finance AI growth. Meta fell 6.98% the next session and its five-year credit default swap spread reached a record. CoreWeave's swaps had already passed 1,000 basis points on October 15, with its 9.75% 2031 bond yielding about 15.6%.

The competing explanation is that this is only a valuation reset. Demand evidence is still strong: Nvidia's chief executive said neocloud demand is off the charts, and QQQ rose 0.50% in the last week while AMD gained 4.77%.

So what: the marginal change is from who can buy chips to who can finance them. Watch the October 28 FOMC, October 29 PCE, credit spreads and Nvidia's November 17 results.

themes.title: Canadian Banks: Rally Into a Rate Hike
themes.status_note: Upgraded to Continuing: all Big Six banks rose in the week as BoC hike odds approached 90%.
themes.summary: Canadian banks are priced for a hiking cycle. ZEB returned +2.60% in one week against +0.18% for the TSX, and +30.19% this year against +14.06%. Every Big Six bank rose in the latest week, led by National Bank and CIBC. The Bank of Canada is expected to raise its policy rate to 2.50% on October 28, which supports lending margins but raises credit costs while unemployment is elevated. September inflation was 3.1%. Continuing, with the decision and RBC's December 3 results as the tests.
themes.body_text:
ZEB, which holds the six largest Canadian banks, closed at C$75.90 on October 27. It gained 2.60% over one week against 0.18% for the S&P/TSX Composite, and 30.19% this year against 14.06%. Its 0.88% one-month gain slightly lagged the index's 1.04%, but all six big banks rose between 1.57% and 3.12% that week.

The driver is monetary policy, not a new earnings release. Swap markets moved from about a 35% chance of an October hike to nearly 90% after Governor Tiff Macklem said on October 17 that the inflation outlook would be quite a bit higher than the July forecast. Statistics Canada reported September inflation at 3.1% on October 19, with gasoline up 27.8% from a year earlier, and the Bank of Canada decides on October 28.

Higher rates help net interest margins, but they also raise borrower stress: unemployment is elevated and the housing market is weak. That is the competing explanation for why the rally may be borrowing future good news.

So what: the sector has price confirmation and breadth, but volume was only 0.35 times its 20-session average. The October 28 decision, the December 9 BoC meeting and RBC's December 3 results are the next evidence.

themes.title: Gold: The War Premium Drains Out
themes.status_note: New: gold is 27% below its January peak and GLD lost 5.4% in a month as real yields stayed high.
themes.summary: Gold's safe-haven premium is unwinding. GLD returned -5.37% over one month against -0.27% for the S&P 500, and -6.06% this year. Gold futures settled at $4,060, about 27% below January's $5,595 peak; silver fell 15.8% and miners 10.4% over the month. The driver is opportunity cost: the Fed hiked in September, December hike odds are about 83%, and real yields remain high even after the 10-year yield slipped below 5%. A one-day bounce is the counterevidence.
themes.body_text:
GLD closed at $372.28 on October 27. It lost 5.37% over one month while the S&P 500 lost 0.27%, and it is down 6.06% this year. December gold futures settled at $4,060, 27% below January's $5,595 peak. Silver fell 15.80% over the month and the miners ETF GDX fell 10.42%, so the move is across the complex rather than one contract.

The first leg was September 28: gold futures settled 3.52% lower as the 10-year yield traded above 5.2% and October hike odds rose to about 70%, less than two weeks after the Fed's September 16 hike to 3.75-4.00%. The second leg was October 22, when GLD fell 2.63% and silver 4.63% while crude stayed near $100 and kept the inflation and hike path alive.

The competing explanation is that this is only a correction: the metal had fallen quickly, and it rose 1.21% on October 27 as oil softened before the Fed.

So what: the marginal buyer now earns a positive real yield in Treasuries. Watch the October 28 FOMC, October 29 PCE and December 9 decision; a dovish surprise or a Hormuz deal that lowers oil would help gold, while a December hike would not.

themes.title: Oil Above $100: The War Supply Premium
themes.status_note: Continuing: XLE gained 9.9% in a month and WTI held near $101; peace-talk headlines cap the premium.
themes.summary: Oil's war premium is still being paid. West Texas Intermediate settled at $101.38 on October 27 and Brent has traded above $110, while XLE returned +9.95% over one month against -0.27% for the S&P 500. Exxon, Chevron and ConocoPhillips each rose more than 10% over the month. The October IEA report still shows supply below demand and inventories far under pre-war levels, but it also cuts its demand forecast. Peace talks knocked oil lower on October 27. Continuing, with volume confirmation absent.
themes.body_text:
West Texas Intermediate settled at $101.38 on October 27, and XLE closed at $68.21. The energy fund gained 9.95% over one month against a 0.27% decline for the S&P 500, and it is up 52.56% this year. Exxon Mobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips gained 12.03%, 11.63% and 16.23% over the same month; this is broad participation, not one name.

Brent settled at $109.86 on October 16 after tanker attacks off Saudi Arabia and Russian refinery strikes, then jumped 4% to $113.17 on October 22. The IEA's October report puts 2026 supply at 100.7 million barrels a day against 102.4 million of demand and says observed inventories remain roughly 500 million barrels below pre-conflict levels.

The competing explanation is demand destruction, which the same IEA report shows, and Goldman Sachs still forecasts Brent near $90 for the fourth quarter. On October 27, talk of Middle East peace talks pushed oil futures down more than 1% and XLE fell 2.05%.

So what: the premium is real but headline-driven. Volume was 0.99 times the prior 20 sessions, so breadth alone does not support High conviction. The next tests are the October 28 EIA inventory report and whether talks produce actual barrels.

themes.title: Long Yields: The Inflation Trade Stalls
themes.status_note: Still Fading: the 10-year fell to 4.99% and TLT gained 2.9% in a month despite hot inflation.
themes.summary: The higher-yield trade has lost its price confirmation. TLT returned +2.91% over one month against -0.27% for the S&P 500, and the 10-year yield is 4.99% after peaking at 5.31% on October 5. On October 22 the yield fell 17 basis points in one session, the largest daily drop since March 2023, as investors bought Treasuries instead of AI shares. Oil above $100 and 3.7% inflation still argue the other way. Fading, with the October 28 FOMC and December hike odds as the test.
themes.body_text:
TLT closed at $81.63 on October 27, up 2.91% over one month while the S&P 500 fell 0.27%. The 10-year yield closed at 4.993%, down from 5.31% on October 5, and the two-year fell to about 4.65% on October 22. That is the opposite of the higher-yield thesis built after the September 16 hike.

The trigger was a haven bid, not softer inflation. On October 22 the 10-year yield fell more than 17 basis points, its biggest one-day decline since March 2023, as AI-related shares sold off and investors moved into government debt. CoreWeave's credit stress and Meta's negative free cash flow made Treasuries look like the safe asset again, even with Brent above $110.

The competing explanation is that the inflation problem has not gone away. Headline CPI was 3.7% in September and oil is above $100; markets still price about an 83% chance of a December hike, which would normally push long yields back up.

So what: price confirmation is absent, so the status stays Fading and conviction is Low. A close back above 5.31% would revive the thesis; a break below 4.9% with a December hike still priced would weaken it further.

proxies.tracking_gap: Duration is roughly 17 years, so it is not a 10-year proxy; it excludes shorter maturities and is exposed to curve shape, not just the 10-year point. Issuer: https://www.ishares.com/us/products/239454/ishares-20-year-treasury-bond-etf

events.title: The 10-year yield fell more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the biggest one-day drop since March 2023, as investors bought havens during the AI-led selloff.
TLT closed at $81.63, down 0.06% while the S&P 500 rose 0.60%, with the 10-year yield at 4.993% before the FOMC.

yesterday_diff.note: Still Fading: since the October 15 snapshot the constraint moved from demand to financing; QQQ fell 3.1% over the month and Meta's negative free cash flow made AI debt the story.
Continuing: XLE added 9.9% over the month as WTI held above $100; the October 27 peace-talk headline cut the premium but not the trend.
Upgraded from Fading to Continuing: all Big Six banks rose in the week as BoC hike odds moved from about 35% to nearly 90%.
Still Fading: the 10-year fell from 5.31% on October 5 to 4.99%, and TLT gained 2.9% over the month despite hot CPI.
New this week: gold is about 27% below its January peak, with silver and miners falling faster over the month as real yields stayed high.
